...all these: from where did they first come? In the middle, where do they all stay? Regarding the end: where do all phenomena of appearance and existence, samsara and nirvana, cease? If one knows through this manner that nothing is established anywhere, then in relation to the past there is no arising; in relation to the future there is no aspiration; in relation to the present there is nothing to identify. Thus, one realizes that from the beginning, one is free from extremes. Furthermore, if there is no arising, what could cease? If there is no arising or ceasing, what could stay? By realizing that it is free from these three—arising, ceasing, and staying—one understands that whatever arises appears as anything, yet in truth, there is nothing to identify. Because these two are not contradictory, one sees the "simplicity" <note>freedom from conceptual elaborations</note>, where arising and liberation are simultaneous. Regarding the analysis through existence and non-existence: is the mind established on the side of existence, or is it established on the side of non-existence? If it is established on the side of existence, examine whether it is established as a shape or color. If it has a shape, examine well whether it is triangular, square, and so forth. If it has a color, examine well whether it is white, black, or whatever. The view of the mind as an existing thing was taught by Naropa, the forefather of the Dakpo Kagyu, through establishing the mode of the body as an existing thing and the mode of the mind as an existing thing...

<leaf-break/>

...the introduction to union <note>of appearance and emptiness</note>, and the establishment of all phenomena as having "one taste" through the example of water and waves. Regarding the first, Lord Lingrepa said: "That experience of last night's dream is a teacher that introduces appearance as mind; I understand." Just as whatever arises in a dream, whether good or bad, happy or unhappy, is the appearance of one's own mind, so too all phenomena of daytime appearance, which appear as good or bad or as diverse things, are not realized to be appearances. In reality, they are in union or of one taste, and nothing exists separately. By this, whatever conditions arise are cut directly, and by leaving the six sense-collections in a relaxed state, the realization of "one taste" or "single taste" arises. Second: just as ice naturally melts in water, so too confusion is liberated in its own place. One does not seek a wisdom separate from knowing the very nature of confusion. As the *Marga-jnana* says: "If the mind is realized, it is Buddha; therefore, one should meditate on the recognition that wisdom is not to be sought elsewhere." And as the glorious Saraha said: "The mind-essence alone is the seed of all, from which samsara and nirvana emanate. I prostrate to the mind that is like a wish-fulfilling jewel, which grants the desired fruits."

<leaf-break/>

Regarding the establishment of this one thing: from the aspect of establishing it, it is named "the Ground." Resting in that state is named "the Path." Obtaining stability in that is named "the Fruit." The essence is self-aware wisdom. The aspect is its appearing everywhere. No one constructed it. Since this has been spontaneously present from the beginning, other than letting it rest in its own place just as it is, there is nothing to be done intentionally. The Regent of the Victorious One <note>Maitreya</note> said: "In this, there is nothing to be cleared away, and not the slightest thing to be added. Look truly at the true itself; once the true is seen, one is completely liberated." The Victorious One himself also said: "In non-existence, there is no meditation. That which is to be meditated upon is not a meditation. Thus, because existence and non-existence are absent, meditation is without an object." These days, the scriptures of the Victorious One and his heirs are recited like the chatter of a parrot, yet people are hostile toward the yoga of "non-mental engagement" and the yoga of "nothing to meditate upon." Forget about the secret of the oral instructions; they do not even lend an ear. As for this meditation on Mahamudra, they disparage it by saying, "There is nothing to be meditated upon here," and so forth. Such compositions...

<leaf-break/>

...the speech that strikes the vital point is very blessed, though some seem to understand it as the words of a madman. Regarding the conclusion of the introduction: identifying Mahamudra and introducing its own nature; cutting off the deviations and mistakes; distinguishing between experience, realization, and understanding; and showing how the three <term>kayas</term> <gloss>bodies of a buddha</gloss> are obtained as the fruit. First, if one asks what Mahamudra is: it refers to the natural mode of being of all phenomena. If one asks where it is established: it is established upon the single mind itself. If one asks what is carried on the path: all phenomena of appearance and sound are carried on the path. If one asks how the fruit is obtained: appearance and existence arise as the play of the three <term>kayas</term>. If one asks how it is carried on the path: as it is said, "Because the mind does not meditate, all beings shall meditate." Without affirming or negating, accepting or rejecting, or focusing on an object with intentionality, one maintains the natural face of the mode of being. This is called "resting in effortless relaxation," "recognizing the natural face in its own place," "obtaining stability in the non-arising and training the skill in the unceasing," and "effortless, authentic mindfulness," or "the path itself..."

࿓࿔།། དེ་ལ་མ་ཡེངས་པ་དེ་གནས་པ་ཡིན་། ཤེབ་ཀྱིས་ཅིའི་ངོ་བོར་ཡང་མ་མཐོང་བ་དེ་རྟོཌ་པ་ཡིན་། གསལ་ལ་མ་འགཌ་པ་སྐད་༡་མའི་ཤེས་པ་དེ་རྩེ་༡་གི་རྣོར་ཡིན་། རིག་

...it is also said. Identify mind as itself. Introduce mind as itself. Recognize mind as itself. Vividly see mind as itself. Experience mind as itself. Conduct oneself as mind itself. Realize mind as itself. Liberate mind as itself. First is that consciousness. Second is ordinary consciousness. Third is the consciousness of the subject. If one recognizes these three, one's own mind is directly identified; the seeing of it is wisdom. The mind-nature is the unfabricated innate. It is the seeing of the authentic essence. This very state, together with realization, is the seeing of the vivid brilliance. In short, it is the total absence of phenomena. It is the very consciousness of a common person. Abandon all the realizations, conducts, and fabricated mental states of the learned. That essence of clear awareness is inseparable, undistracted, and unceasing. Within that state, whatever various memories or thoughts arise, they are all its essence. If ordinary consciousness is not distracted, all memories and thoughts are awareness. One need not view them as faults. It is only when distracted that they are "thoughts," but by looking at that very state, even if one or two thoughts occur, this is the knowledge of everything as mind.
<leaf-break/>
See the nature of the essence. See it as being without seen or seer. See that primordially pure nature as unchanging. See that nature as without increase or decrease. See that nature as without interruption. See that nature as without hope or fear. See one's own mind as simultaneously born. See the innate as the Great Seal. See it directly with the consciousness of the three "seeings." See one's own mind with the eye of knowledge. See it as being without anything to look at or anyone looking. Looking at one's own mind is like a yak looking at itself. Seeing one's own mind for oneself, one is liberated upon seeing it. If one relaxes and does not strive, there is bliss. If one settles without a focal point, there is clarity. If one investigates without accepting or rejecting, there is certainty. If one realizes without abandoning or attaining, there is liberation. The venerable Precious Guru sang the Song of the Great Seal. The verbal instructions of Guru Nyigom: the essence of the awareness of one's own mind, when realized as the essence of the Truth Body, clear and unceasing, and meditated upon without distraction, then the Truth Body is uninterrupted. When certainty and conviction arise like the flow of a river, one never parts from it, and in all conduct...
<leaf-break/>
These words were spoken. One should not show this to everyone, for they will not realize it and it will cause wrong views to arise. These are the precious words requested by Prajnabodhi. There are four causes for the arising of calm abiding: arising from the Guru's blessing, arising from interdependent connection, arising from the accumulation of merit, and arising from the purification of sins. The simultaneously-born wisdom is this very state that is primordially present in ordinary consciousness. To recognize it: leave it unfabricated. Leave it unstained. Leave it naturally as it is. By realizing one's own mind-nature as unborn, unceasing, without location, and without substance, one realizes all appearances and sounds to be the same; that is the view. To remain without distraction from that meaning of mind is meditation. To act with the unborn mind-nature and these appearances/sounds like water and waves is conduct. The best see their own mind as Buddha. The middling see the essence of awareness as unborn. The least rely on cutting through conceptual elaboration and train in one-pointedness. The best realize the mind's essence exactly as it is. The middling realize it without noticing the breath coming and going. The least realize it as being without a body or in equanimity. Regarding the mind:
<leaf-break/>
Remaining undistracted in that is "abiding." Not seeing it as any substance whatsoever with knowledge is "realization." That momentary consciousness, clear and unceasing, is the certainty of one-pointedness. Realizing the essence of awareness as unborn and beyond existence or non-existence is the certainty of freedom from elaboration. Realizing that although things appear as various objects, they are of one essence, is the certainty of one taste. Realizing appearance and emptiness as inseparable and uninterrupted is the Great Equanimity. The essence of mind is like the center of the autumn sky, unchanging, without hope or fear, and unceasing at all times. At the time of training, train in not being distracted from clear awareness. When one becomes habituated to that, certainty arises in oneself. Without losing that essence of mind, one should know all conceptual thoughts and elaborations as mind. Internal signs of calm abiding will come like smoke, like a mirage, like a firefly, like a lamp, or like a cloudless sky. When signs like smoke or a mirage occur, one has gained some power over wisdom. When the internal sign like a lamp occurs at the completion of calm abiding, one has power over wisdom.
